{{Short description|American physicist, educator and book author}}
{{about|the American physicist |other people of the same name|Robert Ehrlich (disambiguation)}}

[[File:Robert Ehrlich (physicist).jpg|thumb|Robert Ehrlich in 2020]]
'''Robert Ehrlich''' (born 1938) is an American physicist.  He has a Bachelor of Science (Φβκ)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pbk.gmu.edu/?page_id=24|title=Officers & Faculty|date=October 17, 2013|website=Phi Beta Kappa}}</ref> from [[Brooklyn College]] (1959), and a Ph.D. in [[physics]] from [[Columbia University]] (1964).  Under his Ph.D. advisor, Nobel Laureate Jack Steinberger, he participated in the Nobel prize-winning [[muon neutrino]] experiment.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Danby |first1=G. |last2=Gaillard |first2=J-M. |last3=Goulianos |first3=K. |last4=Lederman |first4=L. M. |last5=Mistry |first5=N. |last6=Schwartz |first6=M. |last7=Steinberger |first7=J. |title=Observation of High-Energy Neutrino Reactions and the Existence of Two Kinds of Neutrinos |journal=Physical Review Letters |date=1 July 1962 |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=36–44 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.9.36 |bibcode=1962PhRvL...9...36D |hdl=2027/mdp.39015095280841 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>  From 1963 to 1966 he held a postdoctoral position at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] and from 1966 to 1970 he was assistant professor at [[Rutgers University]]. In 1970 he accepted a position as associate professor at [[SUNY New Paltz]], where he served as acting chair of the department of physics. From 1977 until his becoming professor emeritus in 2013, he was professor of physics at [[George Mason University]] in Fairfax, Virginia, having served 15 years as department of physics chair.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://science.gmu.edu/directory/robert-ehrlich|title=Robert Ehrlich {{pipe}} GMU College of Science|website=science.gmu.edu}}</ref>

Ehrlich was elected a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1991, "for application of physics to aspects of the nuclear arms race and contributions to public education in physics".<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=www.aps.org}}</ref>  Ehrlich's primary area of scholarship is [[particle physics]]. He is also well known for his contributions to [[science education]], particularly with simple physics demonstrations and [[computers in the classroom|computer applications]] in [[physics education]]. Another area of his scholarship is energy and the environment, specifically [[nuclear weapon|nuclear arms control]] and [[renewable energy]].  His books have been translated into six languages.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://viaf.org/viaf/64095526/|title=64095526|website=viaf.org}}</ref>

== Publications ==

Other scholars have cited Ehrlich's published books (12 authored, 10 edited) and over 100 articles approximately 800 times. These citations are available via his Google Scholar page (see below under External links).  The list of books and articles can be found here.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ehrlich.physics.gmu.edu/index.php/publications/|title=all publications – The Tachyon Nexus}}</ref>  The books mainly deal with science for the general public, [[physics education]], energy and the [[Natural environment|environment]], and [[nuclear weapon|nuclear arms control]], and most of them are listed below by category.

=== Computers in physics: the CUPS Project ===
Together with his Mason colleague [[Maria Dworzecka]] and [[William M. MacDonald]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.physics.umd.edu/rgroups/ripe/wmm/wmm.html|title = WMM Home Page}}</ref> of the [[University of Maryland]], Ehrlich was a director of the [[National Science Foundation|NSF]]-funded  "Consortium for Upper-Level Physics Software (CUPS)"<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ehrlich |first1=Robert |last2=Dworzecka |first2=Maria |last3=MacDonald |first3=William M. |title=Software Consortium Develops Simulations for Nine Physics Courses |journal=Computers in Physics |date=1992 |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=90 |doi=10.1063/1.4823049 |bibcode=1992ComPh...6...90E }}</ref> The project involved an international team of 29 physicists.  It generated nine books published by [[John Wiley & Sons]] and 27 simulations covering many of the areas of junior-senior courses for undergraduate physics majors. All nine of the books have been translated into Japanese, and one has been translated into Italian.  Three of the simulations have won awards.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Donnelly |first1=Denis |title=CIP's Fourth Annual Software Contest |journal=Computers in Physics |date=1993 |volume=7 |issue=6 |pages=647–654 |doi=10.1063/1.4823240 |bibcode=1993ComPh...7..647D }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Donnelly |first1=Denis |title=CIP's Sixth Annual Software Contest: The Winners |journal=Computers in Physics |date=1995 |volume=9 |issue=6 |pages=594 |doi=10.1063/1.4823449 |bibcode=1995ComPh...9..594D }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Donnelly |first1=Denis |title=CIP's Seventh Annual Educational Software Contest: The Winners |journal=Computers in Physics |date=1996 |volume=10 |issue=6 |pages=532–541 |doi=10.1063/1.4822497 |bibcode=1996ComPh..10..532D |doi-access=free }}</ref> All the programs have now been placed on the Internet Archive Software Collection and can be run from that site.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://archive.org/details/software?query=Consortium+for+Upper-level+Physics+Software|title=Download & Streaming : The Internet Archive Software Collection : Internet Archive}}</ref>  At the invitation of [[UNESCO]], workshops on the CUPS software were conducted in [[Egypt]], [[Jordan]], [[Syria]], and the [[United Arab Emirates]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ehrlich |first1=Robert |last2=Dworzecka |first2=Maria |title=On the Road to Damascus—Technology, Fear, and Fear of Technology |journal=Journal of College Science Teaching |date=1997 |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=179–182 |jstor=42993513 }}</ref>

== Tachyon research and education ==

Since the 1990s, Ehrlich has investigated the possible existence of [[tachyon]]s, that is, hypothetical [[subatomic particles]] that travel faster than the [[speed of light]] in vacuum, especially tachyonic or superluminal neutrinos, about which much has been written.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nu.to.infn.it/Neutrino_Velocity/|title = SuperLuminal Neutrino page (INFN)}}</ref>  He has published extensively in this area,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ehrlich.physics.gmu.edu/index.php/tachyon-papers|title = list of tachyon papers}}</ref> including a 2022 review of all searches for evidence of tachyons.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.3390/sym14061198 | doi-access=free | title=A Review of Searches for Evidence of Tachyons | year=2022 | last1=Ehrlich | first1=Robert | journal=Symmetry | volume=14 | issue=6 | page=1198 | arxiv=2204.12017 | bibcode=2022Symm...14.1198E }}</ref>  Ehrlich is hoping to interest the [[KATRIN]] experiment in conducting a test of his model.  KATRIN's 2019 and 2021 results appear to be consistent with both the standard [[neutrino mass hierarchy]] having three nearly equal mass neutrinos and his exotic 3 + 3 model.  That model, based on an analysis of [[supernova]] [[SN 1987A]] postulates three doublets of active and [[sterile neutrinos]], having specific masses, one of which is tachyonic having m<sup>2</sup> ~ -0.2 keV<sup>2</sup><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Ehrlich|first1=Robert|title=First results of the KATRIN neutrino mass experiment and their consistency with an exotic 3+3 model|journal=Letters in High Energy Physics|date=31 December 2019|volume=2|issue=4|page=139|doi=10.31526/lhep.4.2019.139|arxiv=1910.06158|bibcode=2019LHEP....2..139E|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Ehrlich|first1=Robert|title=The KATRIN neutrino mass results: An alternative interpretation|date=1 September 2021|arxiv=2106.00681}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|arxiv=2204.12017 |last1=Ehrlich |first1=Robert |title=A Review of Searches for Evidence of Tachyons |journal=Symmetry |year=2022 |volume=14 |issue=6 |page=1198 |doi=10.3390/sym14061198 |bibcode=2022Symm...14.1198E |doi-access=free }}</ref>    Ehrlich's model would also be proven right or wrong if a new supernova were to be observed in our galaxy, but these occur only two or three times per century. Supernovae have been observed in other galaxies, but they are so distant that no neutrinos have yet been detected from them. Ehrlich has written a book on tachyons intended for both the general reader and physicists: ''Hunting the Faster than Light Tachyon, and Finding Three Unicorns and a Herd of Elephants'', published by [[CRC Press]], Taylor & Francis Group in 2022.<ref>{{cite book|title= Hunting the Faster Than Light Tachyon, and Finding Three Unicorns and a Herd of Elephants|first=Robert|last=Ehrlich|date=2022|publisher=CRC Press|oclc= 1286422704}}</ref> The book describes the half-century-long search by the author and others for evidence of the reality of tachyons, and more specifically the notion that some neutrinos are tachyons.  Among all the known particles, only neutrinos might be tachyons, because neither their m<sup>2</sup> nor their dv = c - v has ever been definitively observed to be positive.  Ehrlich has also created educational videos about tachyons and [[time travel]], which can be found on his web site "The Tachyon Nexus."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ehrlich.physics.gmu.edu/|title=Home page|date=August 21, 2022|website=The Tachyon Nexus}}</ref>

== Personal life ==

Ehrlich has been married to his wife Elaine since 1961.  They have two sons  and two grandchildren. He is a founding member and Past President of George Mason University's Retired Faculty Association,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://rfa.gmu.edu/|title=Home page|date=August 21, 2022|website=Retired Faculty Association}}</ref> and currently serves as their Webmaster and Program Planning Chair.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://rfa.gmu.edu/about/officers/|title=Officers|date=August 21, 2022|website=Retired Faculty Association}}</ref>
